minutes.headline: Auditor calls finances strong; board pushes a PFAS treatment grant and a cheaper pipeline route
minutes.summary: The district's CPA walked the board through the year's audited financials, calling the district financially strong despite flagging receivables collection as an ongoing challenge and noting an unpaid Medicare tax issue now being corrected. The board spent most of the rest of the meeting on PFAS: resubmitting a state grant application as a construction grant, weighing a cross-country water main route to lower the cost of a future treatment solution, and debating how to respond to a resident's disputed letter to the editor about PFAS and litigation money. No figures were formally voted on beyond routine approval of prior minutes and adjournment.

what_happened.line: The district's auditor called its finances strong overall, but flagged receivables collection and an unpaid Medicare tax matter now being fixed.
The board voted to resubmit its state PFAS grant application as a construction-focused grant rather than the prior form.
The board is weighing a cheaper cross-country water main route and pursuing easements on two properties to lower the cost of a future PFAS treatment system.
A resident asked whether PFAS litigation settlement money is kept separate from regular operating funds.
The board decided to hold off on publicly rebutting a resident's disputed letter to the editor about PFAS until more survey data comes in.

why_it_matters: The PFAS grant resubmission and the pipeline route under discussion will shape how much a future treatment system costs, and how much of that cost lands on water bills.
The Medicare tax correction is headed toward a warrant article, meaning residents may eventually be asked to vote on it.
How the district accounts for PFAS litigation money -- separate from operations or blended in -- bears on how any settlement funds can be used toward treatment costs.
